articles.title: An updated Clairic and Clairic-flash are now open-weight, from the new Workers AI Superintelligence team
articles.excerpt: Clairic graduates from preview, while Clairic-flash joins the repertoire on Workers AI. We’re doing an open-weight release for both extraction models.
details: Cloudflare has become a neolab. We’re building our own frontier AI models for our customers and the open-source community.
Today, we’re announcing two open-weight model releases:

We’re introducing an updated version of Clairic . Since the preview, we’ve improved extraction from complex documents including images and PDFs (new!), with more reliable handling of tables, lists, and dates, and better grounding of answers in the source material.
We’re introducing Clairic-flash , a lighter, faster version of Clairic that delivers strong extraction and prediction performance in a compact, 9-billion-parameter model.
Both extraction models are hosted on Workers AI and full open weights are available on Hugging Face .

articles.title: Internet traffic and attacks during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections
articles.excerpt: On November 3, 2026 U.S. voters headed to the polls. Here’s what Cloudflare data across more than 1,400 protected sites tells us about Election Day Internet traffic and cyberattacks.
details: Visitors to government election websites surged 363% on November 3, the date of the 2026 midterm elections in the United States. Across Cloudflare's election protection programs, we also detected a significant shift in the types and timing of cyberattacks throughout 2026.
Unlike what we saw in other recent elections, attackers focused on gaining access to internal systems and data, rather than knocking websites offline.
Government election websites faced website vulnerability attempts 180 times more often than denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, and at roughly ten times the rate of Cloudflare's broader customer base.
We also found evidence of at least one attempt to exploit a recently disclosed critical PHP vulnerability on a state government voting website in the Western United States.
These attacks peaked in late October, several weeks before the election.

articles.title: Quad9’s withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
articles.excerpt: Quad9's forced withdrawal from France highlights the dangers of mandating DNS-level blocking. We explore why forcing public resolvers to act as content filters is technically flawed and threatens the open Internet.
details: Last month, the Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9 announced that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France. This difficult decision followed months of litigation and a French court ruling that imposed daily financial penalties on Quad9 for failing to block domains associated with alleged copyright infringement.

Quad9’s departure from France is both disheartening and understandable. The court’s ruling put the organization in the impossible bind of having to choose between crippling litigation and penalties, or fundamentally altering its service in a way that would undermine the privacy and security of its users. Left with no good option, Quad9 is choosing the exit door instead.

The withdrawal of a basic infrastructure service from France fundamentally harms the free and open Internet, and it should serve as a warning of the damage that will result if rightsholders and policymakers continue demanding maximal blocking across every layer of the Internet.
It not only deprives French Internet users of a trustworthy and important tool; it creates a real risk of disruption to their daily lives.

Quad9’s resolver is used by a wide variety of individuals and organizations in France - including government bodies, educational institutions, hospitals, and utilities - and Quad9 has no way to directly notify those individuals and institutions that their resolver will soon stop working.

articles.title: Docker patches Java4Shell and the NGINX HTTP/2 with Docker Hardened Images
articles.excerpt: Docker publishes fixed images for both Java4Shell and the NGINX HTTP/2 in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog.
details: OpenJDK and Oracle disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) on November 17, and NGINX released fixes for two HTTP/2 flaws the next day. Docker began publishing fixed images for both in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog starting that same day.

What we know about Java4Shell is that it’s a memory-corruption bug in the Java runtime that can let an attacker with no credentials run code inside a Java application. Many container images contain a Java runtime, including application images that bundle their own, so it affects teams well beyond the ones that write Java.

Docker Hardened Images are the trusted foundation your applications should run on, because a flaw in the runtime inside an image is fixed only when that image is rebuilt, and Docker rebuilds its hardened images as soon as upstream fixes become available.
Fixed images for the Amazon Corretto, SapMachine and Azul Zulu runtimes and for NGINX are in the catalog today, with Eclipse Temurin following as soon as Adoptium completes its fixed builds.
Affected: Java 17.0.6 and later, including Java 21, 25, 26 and 27, from every OpenJDK vendor.

articles.title: Scheduling the removal of the kube-proxy IPVS backend
articles.excerpt: The ipvs backend for kube-proxy was an experiment in providing a service proxy implementation with better performance than the iptables backend. While it succeeded in that goal, the kernel IPVS API has turned out to be a bad match for the Kubernetes Services API, and the ipvs backend was never able to…
details: In Kubernetes 1.29, the project introduced the nftables backend for kube-proxy, which became GA in 1.33.
Part of the plan behind adding the nftables backend was the idea that it would eventually replace both the iptables and ipvs backends.

Because the ipvs backend in particular is complex, not 100% feature complete, and architecturally quite different from the other two backends (and thus more work to maintain), Kubernetes SIG Network decided to officially deprecate it as of Kubernetes 1.35 .
Although it currently remains available in kube-proxy (with a warning about its deprecation), we (Kubernetes SIG Network) now plan to remove it in Kubernetes 1.40.
All ipvs users should therefore be planning to migrate to either the nftables or iptables backends.

articles.title: nginx2root: Five new nginx vulnerabilities, and how Cloudflare protects origins from the worst of them
articles.excerpt: Five memory corruption bugs in nginx, called nginx2root, can let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a server. Here’s how they work, and why origins behind Cloudflare's proxy are shielded from the most serious of these bugs.
details: On November 18, 2026, F5 and nginx.org disclosed ten vulnerabilities in nginx.

Five of them, detailed by the Xint research team and published under the name nginx2root , are memory corruption flaws that an unauthenticated attacker can use to crash an nginx worker or, per Xint's research, run commands on the server.
Xint also found a Linux kernel bug that turns that foothold into root on the host, including from inside a Docker container.

Other teams found the two HTTP/2 bugs independently: F5 also credits Rapid7, Wiz Research and Ikotas Labs for CVE-2026-123007, and Metnir, Wiz Research, and Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for CVE-2026-123633.

nginx is an HTTP web server that also serves as reverse proxy, content cache, load balancer, TCP/UDP proxy server, and mail proxy server. nginx runs a large share of the world's web servers, so this is a patch-now event.

articles.title: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)
articles.excerpt: Java4Shell is a critical memory-corruption flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder that can lead to remote code execution. Cloudflare has released six WAF managed rules for paid plans that logs matching requests by default. Patch your Java runtimes now.
details: On November 17, 2026, the security research company Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) , a memory-corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK, the most widely used Java runtime.
Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical).
OpenJDK published a security advisory and Oracle released patched builds in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update the same day, at 21:00 UTC.
The vulnerability lets a remote attacker with no credentials send malformed Base64 data to a Java application and overwrite memory next to the decoded output.
Calif turned that overwrite into a leak of heap memory, similar to Heartbleed , and into remote code execution.

articles.title: Enabling the parallel frontend on nightly
articles.excerpt: TL;DR: We are enabling the parallel frontend of the Rust compiler on nightly by default, to find remaining issues in preparation for its stabilization. Context The Rust compiler has been using multiple threads to compile code in its "backend" part (using LLVM) for a long time. However, its "frontend" part…
details: The Rust compiler has been using multiple threads to compile code in its "backend" part (using LLVM) for a long time.
However, its "frontend" part (which includes type checking and borrow checking) has been executing sequentially, on a single thread, which of course limits the performance of the compiler.
If you are interested in a more in-depth explanation of parallelism in the Rust compiler, see this previous post .

The compiler frontend actually had support for running in parallel for a long time, but it was not enabled by default due to various issues. Three years ago , we made it possible to opt into the parallel frontend on the nightly channel, with the plan to stabilize it in 2024. Clearly, we did not achieve that goal, but work on the parallel frontend was still slowly progressing in the meantime.
Last year, Vadim Petrochenkov , together with several other contributors, started a coordinated effort to finally get the parallel frontend over the finish line.

articles.title: The best things in open source are built together
articles.excerpt: Introducing Replica and the Open Source Accessibility Framework, new open source projects for collaboration and inclusion. The post The best things in open source are built together appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
details: In 2026, public contributions on GitHub soared to 2.5 billion , more than double last year's total of 1.12 billion. It goes to show how open source remains a powerful mechanism for developers to build, share, and grow communities.

Open source is how I began my GitHub journey. I contributed to Processing Foundation by adding alt-text to images on the p5.js website. This was the first time I felt included in a software development space as someone with a background in traditional fine arts and design. It was the first time I made a fork, opened a pull request, and merged code on a repo that wasn't mine.

Working at GitHub, you hear stories like mine everywhere. Open source is foundational to us not only as a business but also for who we are as the people who build it! We recently launched two new open source projects to share with the community: Replica , an open-source design harness, and the Open Source Accessibility Framework .

I attended John Maeda's session with Qianqian Ye, Director of Creative Technology at Processing Foundation, at GitHub Universe titled, "Sketching with code in the age of AI." This session talked about the power of the open source community and reminded me how important it is to our developer ecosystem.
It is the reason AI tooling understands different coding languages so well, how developers hacked agent harnesses to be more efficient, and why new AI companies have formed.
